quotes.verbatim_quote:
Introduced
here is a 'scale for chording,' and a method of
assigning virtually any chord to one of two
scales—the major 6 diminished and the minor 6
diminished.
quotes.why_load_bearing: This is the foundational methodological claim of the entire chapter, naming the two scales that organize all subsequent chord-movement exercises.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
The misconception that chords are fixed
points in the tune, bound by vertical harmonic
movement, may be the culprit behind the ten-
dency to play the same two or three voicings
over and over for the same change.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Harris names the specific bad habit his method corrects, giving players a diagnostic frame for why movable chords matter.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
This scale is actually comprised of all 3 diminished chords. The
C and A belong to one diminished, the E and G to a second, and the B
diminished chord provides the other four notes of the scale.
quotes.why_load_bearing: Defines the internal architecture of the C6 diminished scale by mapping its eight notes onto three interlocking diminished chords.

quotes.verbatim_quote:
Every minor 7 chord is an inversion of a major 6th chord, and every
minor? flat5 chord is an inversion of a minor 6th chord.
quotes.why_load_bearing: States the two axiomatic equivalences that allow Harris to collapse the m7 and m7b5 chord families into the 6th-chord scales, unifying the harmonic vocabulary.

quotes.verbatim_quote: Remember to move each note to the next note of the scale.
quotes.why_load_bearing: The single mechanical instruction that generates all movable chord progressions in this method.
